  • LIAR-PLUS dataset: Contains fact-checked articles and their justification sentences. EVVER-Net effectively identifies fact-checked evidence with 98.5% classified as fact-checked.
  • MOCHEG dataset: Combines data from Politifact and Snopes. EVVER-Net correctly classifies 83.6% as fact-checked.
  • FACTIFY dataset: Contains textual and image claims linked to reliable documents. Claims are classified as support, insufficient, or refute. The support and insufficient classes were collected from credible sources, while articles in the refute class were collected from fact-checking websites. EVVER-Net classification reveals that 88% of the contents categorized as support or insufficient are classified as credible, whereas 95% of the documents in the refute class are fact-checked.
  • NewsCLIPpings+ dataset: Contains web-sourced external textual evidence linked to image-caption pairs. Textual evidence was obtained by querying images in inverse search mode using the Google Vision API. EVVER-Net classified 64.5% of the evidence as credible, 21.4% as unreliable, and 14.1% as fact-checked. Despite the majority of evidence being considered credible, the presence of some pieces sourced from unreliable or leaked origins may compromise accuracy and introduce unrealistic elements into the assessment process.
  • VERITE dataset: Contains image-caption pairs categorized as ‘True’, ‘Miscaptioned’, and ‘Out-of-Context’. ‘Miscaptioned’ pairs sourced from fact-checked articles like Snopes and Reuters were considered. Misleading claims along with their images were collected, and the Google API was used to retrieve textual and visual evidence. EVVER-Net classified 42.6% as credible, 35.3% as fact-checked, and 22.1% as unreliable. The high fact-checked rate is attributed to ‘Miscaptioned’ claims sourced from fact-checked articles, often returning leaked evidence via Google API searches. For ‘Out-of-Context’ pairs, fact-checked rates dropped to 14.5%, while unreliable evidence increased to 27.3%. These claims come from fact-checked articles but the out-of-context images are retrieved from the Web, and subsequently used to retrieve textual info from Google API, increasing unreliable evidence likelihood.

considerations.use_case: EVVER-Net supports fact-checking, credibility assessment, and misinformation detection in news content. It is designed for researchers, journalists, and platforms needing scalable evidence verification.

eval_set.motivation: We evaluated EVVER-Net on a variety of datasets, including text-only, multimodal, and Web-sourced collections. These datasets feature fact-checked articles and external evidence, simulating real-world misinformation detection tasks. The Domain Credibility Score (DCS) was not used, as domain information was unavailable. Instead, we focused on the model’s ability to assess credibility based on content and supporting evidence. Evaluations were conducted in three stages: text datasets, multimodal datasets, and datasets aggregating evidence from the Web.

model.author: CERTH - The Centre for Research & Technology, Hellas
model.name: EVVER-NET
model.overview: EVVER-Net is a text classification model that filters unreliable or leaked evidence in automated fact-checking systems. Trained on the CREDULE dataset, it classifies input texts as Credible, Unreliable, or Leaked. The model supports both short and long documents and uses domain credibility scores to boost accuracy. It improves fact-checking pipelines by removing biased or low-quality sources before verification.
model.version:
1. Short-text model: Based on headlines/titles (T5, DeBERTa, CLIP)
  2. Long-text model: Full article content (Longformer, LongT5)
  3. DCS-enhanced model: Combines text with domain-level credibility scores

training_set.datasets: We construct the CREDULE (CREDible, Unreliable or LEaked) dataset, spanning the years 2016 to 2022, for a total of 91,632 articles (Fact-checked (30,209), Credible (31,230), and Unreliable (30,193)) by modifying, merging, and extending MultiFC, Politifact, PUBHEALTH, NELA-GT, FakeNewsCorpus, and Getting Real About Fake News. These established datasets contain short texts (titles) as well as the long texts (full articles) of the news articles. We extract the article bodies, where they are not given, and other meta-data to better balance the classes. The final CREDULE dataset consists of 91,632 pieces, equally distributed in three classes: “Credible”, “Unreliable”, and “Fact-checked” (or Leaked). We augment CREDULE by integrating external domain credibility scores (DCS) from the Media Bias/Fact Check (MBFC) website.
training_set.motivation: Automated fact-checking (AFC) systems that incorporate external information from the Web often retrieve evidence that include leaked content—text originating directly from fact-checking websites—as well as information from unreliable outlets. These types of evidence can lead to unrealistic evaluation settings for early misinformation detection or undermine the effectiveness of the AFC system respectively. To address this, we constructed the CREDULE dataset (CREDible, Unreliable, or LEaked), which includes 91,632 articles labeled according to their reliability and origin. This dataset enables targeted training of models that can distinguish between credible, unreliable, and leaked evidence, supporting the development of AFC systems that operate more reliably in real-world conditions. Each article entry includes its title, publication date, URL, assigned topic, and classification label. The dataset exhibits balanced distribution across all classes in terms of articles per year, topics, and title lengths.
training_set.pre_processing: For feature extraction, we utilize the [CLS] token to capture contextual information and train our classifier.
